text: This is doeff: algebraic effects for Python. Here is a small card battle, written once.
The battle only says what it needs: a random number, the player's move, a line for the screen, and a count of each card played.
Each yield hands an effect outward. The battle never says who rolls the dice or who plays the cards.
Layer one: a scripted player, seeded dice, and a screen that prints.
Run it, and the fight prints turn by turn.
It ends in a win on turn six. Nothing in battle changed. Only the handlers around it.
Layer two: swap the player for a random bot. Same battle, same dice seed, and it wins on turn four.
Layer three: record. A handler keeps every dice roll and every choice on a tape. This fight left thirty-two answers.
Replay answers from the tape, with no dice and no player. The same fight, the same result.
Layer four: a Monte Carlo bot. To choose a card, its handler plays out the rest of the fight, again and again.
That handler runs battle itself, under dice and a random bot, and keeps the move that wins most often.
A program is a value, so a handler can run it. On the same seed, this bot also wins on turn four.
Layer five: a hundred fights in parallel, one task for each seed. Spawn them, then gather the results.
The random bot wins seventy-three of a hundred.
The Monte Carlo bot wins all one hundred. Same battle, different layers.
doeff: algebraic effects for Python. From a scripted test to a bot that searches, stack the layers you need around the same code. pip install doeff.
